content.text:
Every Wizard subclass in the 2024 Player’s Handbook is themed around a
	specific school of magic, seeking to emphasize and improve spells in that
	school. While you’re not locked into learning specific spells, you’ll
	typically benefit more by focusing on spells from your chosen school than by
	picking whatever spells catch your fancy.
For legacy subclasses, see our
2014 Wizard Subclasses Guide

content.text: The advice in this article is based on the current
State of the 2024 DnD Character Optimization Meta

as of when the article was last updated. Keep in mind that the state of the meta periodically changes as new source materials are released, and the article will be updated accordingly as time allows. Also be sure to check for
errata
periodically.
We will not include 3rd-party content, Unearthed Arcnaa content, or homebrew in guides for official content because we can’t assume that your game will allow them.

The Abjurer Wizard’s signature mechanic is Arcane Ward, which provides a pool
	of not-quite-hit-points that you can use to mitigate huge amounts of damage to
	yourself and eventually to your allies. Spell Breaker makes the Abjurer the
	uncontested champion of Counterspell and Dispel Magic, allowing you to defend
	your allies both from mundane damage with your ward and from spells with
	Counterspell and Dispel Magic. While this is undeniably effective, the purely
	reactive nature of the subclass can make it boring to play for many players
	who prefer a more proactive approach to challenges.

items.text:
: Free spells in your
		spellbook. Always nice, but not massively impactful.

: A great way to protect
		yourself and your party. The ward works a lot like Temporary Hit Points,
		but, since they aren’t technically THP, the two effects provide two layers
		of protection before you take real hp damage. The Ward itself begins at full
		HP the first time you cast an Abjuration spell each day. Mage Armor is a
		great way to get the ward in place before you go anywhere dangerous.

Since the ward can take damage in your place, you may even be able to
			avoid saves to maintain Concentration when you take damage. This
			additional overshield is a resource, and resources are meant to be spent,
			but don’t be reckless and overextend yourself. Be sure to take all the
			normal defensive precautions and the ward will help mitigate damage when
			the dice just don’t go in your favor.

Remember that damage to the ward is applied after damage resistances, so
			anything that reduces the incoming damage will stretch the value of your
			ward. Blade Ward and Resistance can both help here, though you may want to
			Concentrate on more impactful spells.

Unfortunately, charging the ward requires you to cast Abjuration spells
			using spell slots, which makes it difficult and expensive to keep the ward
			fully charged throughout the day. Look for Abjuration buffs that you can
			cast on your allies before jumping into combat.

: Your party’s Defender
		likely takes a lot more damage than you, so soaking some of it with your
		ward can really cut down on how many resources your party must devote to
		healing. Just be aware that you’ll be unable to cast Shield, Absorb
		Elements, and Counterspell in response to future triggering events should
		you block some damage to an ally since you only get one Reaction per
		round.

: Two free prepared spells,
		and, if you cast either and fail the ability check, your spell slot isn’t
		expended. Counter every hostile spell worth a spell slot even if you’re
		unlikely to succeed. Outside of combat, you can repeatedly cast Dispel Magic
		at level 3 until you eventually get lucky on the check.

In combat, the ability to cast Dispel Magic as a Bonus Action will rarely
			be impactful, but, against enemy spellcasters, it’s a powerful way to
			strip them of buff spells.

: Resistance to spells is
		great for resisting dangerous save or suck spells, and resistance to spell
		damage makes you greatly resistant to direct damage spells which typically
		don’t require saves (Eldritch Blast, Fire Bolt, etc.). Both halves of the
		feature apply at the same time, so against spells which allow you to save
		for reduced damage (Fireball, etc.), this is extremely effective because on
		a successful save you’ll often take just a quarter of the game. However,
		you’re expected to counter spells rather than try to resist them, so this is
		mostly a redundant defense for when you’re outnumbered or surprised.

content.text:
The Bladesinger is a fun gish build, focused more on spellcasting than gish
	options like the the Eldritch Knight does, and allowing you to dive into melee
	combat while still using the full Wizard spell list. Bladesong’s features do a
	lot to improve the Wizard’s durability.

The biggest problem with the Bladesinger is that it’s at its best when used
	purely defensively. Bladesong is an exceptional defensive buff, but the best
	thing that you can do with your turn in any given situation is to ignore your
	subclass and go straight to the Wizard’s spell list. Extra Attack exists, but
	adding an unmodified weapon attack to your Action isn’t hugely better than
	just casting a Cantrip, and Wizards have so many good offensive spells that
	resorting to Cantrips is best used to conserve resources when a fight has
	largely run its course but you still need to clean up the last few enemies.

Despite all that, the Bladesinger is still really fun to play. While we don’t
	think the subclass is as powerful as other Wizard subclasses, it’s still very
	effective and a whole lot of fun.

items.text:
: The defining feature of the
		class, Bladesong is a powerful buff that tries to turn a Wizard into a gish.
		Adding intelligence to everything makes that fairly effective, especially
		since you can get your AC and Concentration saves much higher than most
		builds can. You also get additional move speed, which helps you get yourself
		closer to the things that can attack into your stacked AC.

Bladesong, combined with high Dexterity and buffs like Shield, allows the
			Bladesinger to boost their AC to heights that most classes simply can’t
			match without magic items. However, you’re still vulnerable to other
			sources of damage like spells and area of effect damage, so bring other
			defensive options like Absorb Elements and Counterspell. Also remember
			that a single critical hit could easily take you out of combat unless you
			can also use Song of Defense to reduce the damage enough to keep yourself
			going.

Since your uses of Bladesong per day are tied to your Intelligence
			Modifier, you need to think of this more as an occasional buff than your
			go-to option in combat. Use this as-needed primarily as a defensive buff
			and pretend that you’re any other type of wizard until you pick up Extra
			Attack and your Intelligence Bonus increases.

: A significant bonus to your
				AC. A Bladesinger with Mage armor and high Dexterity and Intelligence
				can easily stack their AC very high, especially with Shield available
				for anything that still manages to hit you.

: You still need good
				Dexterity to support your AC, but your Intelligence will outpace your
				Dexterity for most of your career, and this removes the need to rush
				both scores to 20.

: A huge improvement to your
				Concnetration. If you get proficiency in Constitution saves and/or War
				Caster to get Advantage, you can make your Concentration nearly
				untoushable.

: Better weapon
		proficiencies and an extra skill, through the skill options are
		disappointing. You only get martial melee weapons, but strongly consider
		multiclassing to get proficiency in martial ranged weapons. A Bladesinger
		with a pistol is very effective, especially if you have Weapon Mastery.

: One of your attacks can be a
		replace by a Cantrip, so you can use Booming Blade/Green-Flame
		Blade/Swordburst/True Strike and make an additional weapon attack using one
		Action. You get all the effectiveness of using an attack Cantrip without
		giving up the multiple attacks made by using Extra Attack, so you get the
		best of both options.

Consider carrying a decent ranged weapon like a crossbow so that on turns
			when you plan to use a ranged attack Cantrip you can make a ranged weapon
			attack in the same turn.

Since you’re taking the Attack action to use this, it’s compatible with
			anything that relies on the Attack action, such as the Dual Wielder feat.
			You could use a Light weapon and Dual Wielder to make a total of 3 regular
			weapon attacks plus cast a Cantrip in a signle turn. Add Conjure Minor
			Elementals to mix and you have very reliable damage output at minimal
			resource cost.

: This is a fine way to
		pad your d6 hit points, but it will eat through your spell slots very
		quickly. Consider Absorb Elements and Shield as your go-to options for
		mitigating damage, but if Shield won’t negate an attack you might use this
		instead if you expect the damage to be more than you’re willing to take or
		if you’re worried about losing Concentration on a spell.

content.text:
Mostly focused on summoning, but with a little splash of teleportation, the
	Conjurer masters summoning creatures to fight alongside them. Their features
	makes it easier to keep your summons on the field, allowing you to stretch the
	impact of your spells. Summon spells are already powerful, providing an
	expendable damage sponge and reliable damage output while leaving your action
	economy free, and further enhancing that capability makes them even better.

While Wizards don’t get Summon X spells until level 3 spells, Battle Familiar
	is a level 2 Conjuration spell which can either summon an independent creature
	or buff your existing Familiar, serving essentially the same function as a
	normal summon spell so that you can start summoning earlier. Battle Familiar
	also doesn’t require Concnetration, which is unusual for a summoning spell,
	and allows you to use it alongside another summoning spell. As you add
	subclass features, Durable Summons and Splintered Summons make it actively
	destrimental to have a pre-existing familiar, so it’s a better idea to dismiss
	your familiar so that you can summon better combat monsters.

items.text:
: Short-range
		teleportation without a spell slot a few times per day, and you can even use
		it to swap places with a willing ally. If you’re in a dangerous position,
		you might use this to swap places with a more durable ally (or at least with
		a more expendable one).

: Free spells in your
		spellbook. Always nice, but not massively impactful.

: More range on
		Benign Transposition, and you gain the ability to turn spell slots into
		extra uses. A level 3+ slot is very expensive, so consider if it makes more
		sense to cast Misty Step (level 2) instead.

: A significant improvement
		to the durability of your summoned/created creatures. Obviously this applies
		to Summon X spells, but it also applies to familiars from Find Familiar.
		Since familiars are frail by default, the THP is a huge improvement to the
		durability of CR 0 beasts which typically have single-digit hit points.

Unfortunately, the THP here won’t stack with the Temporary Hit Points
			from Battle Familiar, and the damage resistance only applies while the THP
			from Durable Summons are in effect. When you cast Battle Familiar to
			enhance an existing familiar, you’ll need to decide which pool of THP you
			want to retain. If you summon a fresh familiar, Durable Summons applies
			normally, so that’s likely the better option.

Since this only works with Conjuration spells, it won’t work with spells
			like Animate Dead, Tiny Servant, or Animate Objects.

: You’re most likely
		concentrating on a summon spell at all times in combat, so losing
		Concentration means losing your central tactic. If your only Concentration
		spells are combat spells (possible, but unwise), this effectively makes you
		immune to losing Concentration to damage.

: Your summoned
		creatures’ hit points are halved, but they get the THP from Durable Summons,
		which singificantly mitigates that cost. You’re doubling your damage output
		at the cost of a few hit points.

You get this once per Long Rest for free, and with the 1-hour duration of
			summon spells, you should be able to drag your summons through 2 or 3
			fights in a dungeon situation. Spending a level 5+ spell slot to use this
			again is very costly, but it’s absolutely worth the price.

This notably applies to Battle Familiar, too, which feels like an
			oversight. Battle Familiar doesn’t require Concentration, so you can use
			another summon spell like Summon Aberration at the same time. If you spend
			the spell slot to reuse Splintered Summons, you could have a total of 4
			summoned creatures at the same time. It’s incredibly resource-intensive to
			do so, but in a hard fight it’s hard to deny the effectivness of summon an
			entire adventuring party worth of combat monsters.

content.text:
Forewarned is fore-armed, and Divination is all about forewarning. If you
	ever walk into a room without knowing who and what is inside it, you aren’t
	casting enough Divinations. The biggest problem with relying heavily on
	Divinations is that they can quickly eat your spell slots, often with little
	tangible effect. Fortunately, Expert Divination dramatically reduces the cost
	of casting divination spells. Portent provides a wonderful mechanic to
	influence rolls, allowing you alter the outcome of critical rolls in
	significant and powerful ways.

As great as Portent is, if you plan to play a Diviner, you and your DM need
	to be prepared to handle divinations and how they work. The DM may be forced
	to predict the future for you, to offer cryptic hints, or to improvise the
	idle activities of creatures who are generally just sitting in a room waiting
	for your party to come fight them. You need to remember to use your Divination
	spells to mitigate risk and to solve problems that can’t be solved using
	Fireball and the like. But, if you put in the work, the Diviner Wizard will
	reward you for your efforts.

items.text:
: Free spells in your
		spellbook. Always nice, but not massively impactful.

: Roll high? Save it for important
		saving throws or attacks. Roll low? Use it to replace an enemy attack roll
		or an enemy saving throw. There is no way for this to be bad unless you
		forget to use it. Portent is School of Divination’s signature trait, and
		mastering it will have a massive impact on your game.

: This dramatically
		expands the number of spells you can cast in a day. If you ever think “is it
		worth a spell slot to cast a Divination right now?”, the answer should
		always be “yes”. Throw them around like confetti. You can even use Mind
		Spike (the only damage-dealing divination spell in the game) to get big
		piles of single-target damage at minimal cost whenever you might normally
		use a cantrip.

: The wording is odd. You gain the ability
		listed in the bullet until your next rest. For example: the “See
		Invisibility” option gives you the ability to cast See Invisibility without
		spending a spell slot, but you still need to actually do so.

: Darkvision isn’t a
				Divination, so this is a good way to get it for free if you don’t get it
				from your race, an item, or an ally who can cast Darkvision.

: Cast Comprehend
				Languages as a Ritual.

: See Invisibility is
				essentially. It has a 1-hour duration, but you can cast it without
				spending a spell slot, so you can freely refresh the duration whenever
				you’re out of combat.

: Not a game changer, but
		Portent is fantastic, and this makes it 50% more powerful.

: Wizards
		typically dump Charisma and don’t have any Charisma skills on their class
		skill list, which makes it hard for them to be your party’s Face, but this
		closes that gap. Unfortunately, you only get one skill with the Intelligence
		bonus, so you’ll still want a bit of Charisma if you plan to play your
		party’s Face.

Because the bonus is on top of your Charisma modifier, you have the
			potential for an unusually high skill modifier here. If you’re leaning
			into Face skills heavily, consider levels in Bard or Rogue for Expertise.
			Throw in Enhance Ability (Charisma), and you’re basically unstoppable.

: Free spells in your
		spellbook. Always nice, but not massively impactful.

: A powerful save-or-suck
		effect without a spell slot, but it does have some important limitations.
		Relying on the Charmed condition means that some creatures will be resistant
		or immune, and the 10-foot range means that you need to be dangerously close
		to your enemy. If you have nothing more important to do, take advantage of
		your target’s incapacitation to put them in chains/manacles/ropes if you
		don’t need your actions for something more important.

This notably doesn’t require Concentration, so you could use this on
			multiple targets and you can cast other spells without breaking it.

: This applies to
		frustratingly small number of spells: Charm Person/Monster, Enhance Ability,
		Hold Person/Monster, Tasha’s Hideous Laughter, and Tasha’s Mind Whip. Adding
		an additional creature is great for those spells, but that is a tiny sliver
		of your capabilities.

: Potentially negate or
		retarget a successful enemy attack. Melee attacks may make it harder to
		retarget because your enemy may only have a single target in reach, but
		ranged attacks can frequently offer numerous target. Because the retargeted
		attack uses the original attack roll, this is especially potent when used on
		crits.

The recharge mechanic here is unusual. Instead of spending a spell slot
			to reuse it or having a limited pool of uses, you recharge Instinctive
			Charm by casting an Enchantment spell with a spell slot. If you’re using
			Enchantment spells consistently in combat, you can easily keep this at the
			ready at all times.

: Most non-combat spells
		which impose the Charmed condition (Charm Person, etc.) let the target know
		that they were Charmed when the spell ends, which often comes with social
		consequences. Removing that drawback for one creature makes it much easier
		to use those spells.

The second hand of the spell lets you erase hours of a target’s memories.
			You could charm or even dominate a creature, have them tell you everything
			they know, help you do stuff, maybe even harm their allies, then whipe
			your target’s memory. It’s unlikely to be useful in combat, but it’s
			fantastically powerful outside of combat.

content.text:
Evocation is the blunt hammer of magic, and the Evoker Wizard swings it
	better than anyone. It’s rarely subtle or elegant, and it’s often imprecise.
	But, hey, when 90% of problems are nails, the hammer is the king of tools. The
	Evoker is a great option for players who are new to spellcasters because many
	of the Evoker’s best spells are mechanically simple, and the subclass makes it
	extremely reliable.

items.text:
: Free spells in your
		spellbook. Always nice, but not massively impactful.

This feature is notably not limited to Wizard cantrips, in case you
			happen to have something from another class, a feat, or a Species
			trait.

: Friendly fire happens
		inevitably when you have an Evoker in the party. This goes a long way to cut
		down on the problem, and you should abuse the fact that your allies are
		functionally immune to your spells wherever possible.

There’s some weird nuance here that’s easy to overlook: While this is
			clearly intended to protect allies from Burning Hands, Fireball, and other
			such AOE damage options, the protection doesn’t end after the initial
			effect of the spell. Creatures are protected from the spell’s effects for
			the spell’s full duration.

This means that your allies can comfortably walk around in the areas of
			spells like Sickening Radiance, potentially dragging enemies about inside
			the area to force them to take damage. You could even cast Otiluke’s
			Freezing Sphere, designate your allies as protected by Sculpt Spells, then
			send them off with pockets full of frozen spheres to smash at their feet
			in a room full of enemies. Honestly, I don’t think this was intended when
			WotC wrote School of Evocation. Much like Empowered Evocation, I think
			that they meant for Sculpt Spells only to apply to the initial effects.
			But it’s been 5+ years and we haven’t gotten errata or tweets from Jeremy
			Crawford, so it appears that Sculpt Spells works as I’ve described it
			until someone tells us otherwise.

: This is a
		considerable damage boost. However, it only applies to one damage roll, so
		any spell that rolls damage multiple times (e.g. Magic Missile) won’t
		benefit from this repeatedly. Instead, focus on multi-target instantaneous
		damage spells like Acid Splash and Chain Lightning.

: This is a great way to get
		more mileage out of reliable lower-level spells like Magic Missile and
		Fireball at a level where your higher-level spells and spell slots would
		generally eclipse them. Just be sure to have a Cleric handy when you start
		intentionally taking damage.

Because this only applies on the turn that you cast the spell, it doesn’t
			significantly benefit spells that deal ongoing damage like Wall of Fire or
			Sickening Radiance.

content.text:
Illusion is the most complex, open-ended, and flexible school of magic. It is
	limited only by your and your DM’s imaginations. A clever player and patient
	DM willing to play along can make the Illusionist an unstoppable creative
	force. However, subjective interpretations of NPC behavior can also make the
	Illusionist a frustrating, ineffective nightmare. If you plan to play an
	Illusionist, have a thorough discussion with your DM about how they want to
	handle illusions before you commit.
DnD 5.5 Illusionist Wizard Subclass Guide

items.text:
: Free spells in your
		spellbook. Always nice, but not massively impactful.

can be
		incredibly powerful in the hands of a smart caster, and adding both effects
		on one casting makes it considerably more useful. Creating an illusion of a
		pot lying on the floor accompanied by the sound of a pot falling, or an
		illusion of a small animal accompanied by appropriate sounds (I’m fond of
		chickens for this purpose) can be excellent distractions, and creatures
		don’t get a save or a skill check to disbelieve the illusion until they
		spend an Action to do so.

While it’s primarily a non-combat utility, the ability to cast Minor
			Illusion as a Bonus Action makes it an exciting tool in combat, too.
			Creating visual cover to break lines of sight can have a huge impact.
			Depending on how your DM handles illusions, you may be able to hide
			yourself inside an object like a crate or a barrel to make yourself
			untargetable.

Don’t overlook the range increase, either. 60 feet of additional range
			means that you can do illusory nonsense from a safe distance, such as
			leading enemies far away from you and your party in order to avoid violent
			encounters.

Changing the spells’ school to Illusion has no mechanical benefit on its
			own, but remember that Improved Illusions increases the range of your
			Illusion spells by 60 feet, allowing you to cast these spells from up to
			150 feet away.

Two free summon spells is pretty nice. Summon Beast and Summon Fey both
			offer some appealing options, and upcasting summon spells to boost their
			stats and number of attacks keep them relevant for your whole career.

The two free castings (one for each summon) are a nice convenience,
			giving you low-cost canon fodder that can absorb a few hits that might
			otherwise target you and your allies. The summons won’t last long in
			combat with half hit points, but both spells have a 1-hour duration, so
			you can pre-cast them and wander around outside of combat with a pet ready
			to go. Even as you gain levels and a level 2 or level 3 summon stops being
			a threat, they can still be useful as a scout or as a distraction.

: Infallibly ignore one
		attack against you for free, once per Short or Long Rest. Very good for a
		squishy Wizard. Combined with other defensive measures like hiding and using
		cover, you may even be able to forgo Shield, especially since you can use
		this again at the cost of a level 2 spell slot.

: This turns your
		illusions into creation spells, which means that any tool that you can
		imagine is available for the low cost of casting Silent Image. Sadly,
		Malleable Illusions likely doesn’t let you change the object which you’ve
		chosen to make real because Illusory Reality only applies when you cast the
		spell.

You can’t directly harm creatures with Illusory Reality, but the rules
			say nothing about impeding, restraining, blocking, or even dropping them.
			Throw up a Silent Image to create a wall of stone between you and your
			foes, or to put a cage around them. Create an illusory bridge with a
			convenient trap door (or just time it so that they’re on the bridge when
			the 1-minute duration expires) and drop your enemies into a pit.

content.text:
The DnD 5.5 Necromancer Wizard delivers on the fantasy of controlling an army
	of undead thralls. The subclass empowers both summoned and permanently created
	undead, making them more durable, more dangerous, and more numerous, while
	also emphasizing your necromancy spells so that you lean heavily into the
	theme and mechanics and be rewarded for doing so. The subclass has several
	very satisfying interactions between subclass features and spells, and a
	well-prepared and clever player can make it extremely powerful beyond the base
	power of any given feature.

The biggest problem for the Necromancer is that DnD doesn’t gracefully handle
	the exact playstyle that the Necromancer is built to support. Bringing a bunch
	of additional creatures that you control into a fight can quickly bog down the
	game, and many enemies simply don’t have a way to handle crowds, so
	surrounding enemies with expendable bodies essentially ends a fight. While
	this is exactly the fantasy that we want from a necromancer, it may lead to a
	frustrating experience at the table.

If you plan to play a Necromancer Wizard, read our advice here thoroughly and
	talk to your table about it beforehand. If the whole table is on board, you
	could have a great time! But if you grind the the game to a halt because
	skeletons 4 thorugh 27 need to miss a series of attacks one at a time, it’s
	going to be a problem for everyone involved, including you. At the same time,
	if you don’t use permanent undead, you’re basically playing a spooky Conjurer.
	Again: talk to your table and be sure that everyone is on board, and be
	prepared to make compromises for the health of the game.

In the DnD 5.5 rules, Animate Dead and Create Undead give players the ability
	to create and command permanent undead minions, and the Necromancer Wizard
	leans into that capability, so it’s an expected part of the subclass’s
	playstyle. Maintaining control of your undead requires you to recast Animate
	Dead/Create Undead every 24 hours, which means that you’re effectively
	committing that spell slot to the undead which it created for as long as you
	plan to keep them. You could commit every spell slot of level 3 and above to
	this, maximizing the size of your undead army at the cost of all of your other
	capabilities.

While that’s certainly tempting, it’s unwise. Your undead army is a hammer,
	and not every problem is a nail. Try using Arcane Recovery as a guideline for
	how much to commit to your permanent undead so that you don’t stretch yourself
	too thin. You might want more minions than that, and that’s fine, but it’s a
	good starting point while you feel out what works for your and your party.

Bringing an army to a game which typically focuses on a party of around 4
	players comes with some complications. Handling a crowd of undead can slow
	down the game significantly, requiring you to track more turns, more attacks,
	and more pools of hit points. It can easily be a nightmare at the table. To
	simplify things, talk to your DM about having your undead take their turns in
	groups and use the Handling Mobs rules from the 2014 DMG to handle their
	attacks instead of rolling for their attacks inidividually. This will
	singificantly reduce the negative impacts on the game while still letting you
	command your horde of shambling corpses.

items.text:
: Several excellent features. Oddly,
		this specific feature doesn’t require you to hold your spellbook even though
		several of the Necromancer’s other subclass features do.

: Damage
				resistances are always great. Necrotic damage isn’t common at low
				levels, but it becomes more common at high levels.

: This is a miniscule
				amount of healing. It would be enough to heal dying allies, but this
				only affects undead. There aren’t currently any playable undead species
				and only a tiny handful of options can make players undead at high
				levels. You’re more likely going to use this on your own undead minions,
				including your familiar, and most of those will be destroyed when they
				hit 0 hp. The impact here will be very minor.

Once you start creating permanent undead minions, this may be more
					helpful. Using Animate Dead to creat eskeletons gives you creatures
					with a single Hit Point Die, which doesn’t give them much built-in
					healing, especially when you buff their hit point maximum with Grave
					Resilience. If you have damage undead, you can have them stand at a
					safe distance and use this to heal them while you’re busy fighting,
					then rotate them back to the front lines when they’re sufficiently
					healed.

: Your first taste of
				having an undead minion! Making your familiar undead lets you heal it
				with Grim Harvest and lets it benefit from the Necromancer’s
				higher-level subclass features.

The ability for your familiar to attack in your stead when you take
					the Attack action is exciting, but has some complications. Because
					familiars roll their own initiative, your familiar’s turn may be
					significantly separated from yours. Your familiar might move into
					position to attack, then several creatures might act before you can
					act and take the Attack action. Enemies might move away or your
					familiar might be destroyed. Your best bet is to Ready an Attack for
					when your familiar moves into reach to attack.

Beyond the frustrating timing, you also need a familiar that has
					meaningful attacks. Your familiar options are CR 0 beasts plus
					Skeleton and Zombie. CR 0 beasts will typically have attack bonuses of
					+4 at the absolute best and will deal very little damage, typically at
					most 1d6 damage. That’s pitiful compared to a Cantrip which you could
					cast with the same Action that you would use to Attack.

The Skeleton and Zombie are both CR 1/4, so they’re at least
					marginally better than existing familiar options. They have better
					attack bonuses (+5 for both), more hit points (13 and 15,
					respectively) than the 2 to 5 hit points familiars typically have,
					they have opposable thumbs, and they may be able to use equipment
					intended for humanoids. Skeletons wear armor and use weapons by
					default, so your DM might let you upgrade their gear.

If you want your familiar to attack, the Skeleton is the better
					choice. They have a ranged attack, and that alone solves a lot of
					problems. If you want a familiar that can survive taking a few hits,
					you want the Zombie. Undead Fortitude will make it difficult for many
					enemies to keep down. When it stands back up at 1 hp, remember that
					you can heal it with Grim Harvest. It’s not a lot, but it will reduce
					the DC for the next save your zombies makes for Undead Fortitude.

If you’re leaning into your familiar, storngly consider the Familiar
					Friend feat. The additional hit points will keep your familiar on the
					field longer, and you can cast Find Familiar once per day without a
					material component, which makes it less annoying to have your familiar
					destroyed. The other familiar feats (Elemental Familiar, etc.) may
					also be appealing.

Also strongly consider the Battle Familiar spell. If you cast it
					while you have your undead familiar summoned, they retain their
					creature type, so they’ll continue to benefit from some of your
					subclass features. Grim Harvest won’t do anything for the THP granted
					by the spell, unfortunately.

: Free spells in your
		spellbook. Always nice, but not massively impactful.

: Remember that these
		features only apply while you are holding your spellbook. Spellbooks aren’t
		a Spellcasting Focus unless you have a magic item like an Arcane Grimoire,
		so you’ll frequently need to commit one hand to your spellbook and your
		other hand to a Spellcasting Focus or leave it empty to handle spell
		components.

: Remove 1 level of
				Exhaustion a day. Only situationally useful, but it does mean that you
				could forgo eating and use Grave Resilience to negate the penalty for
				doing so. There’s little benefit to doing so, but it is an option.

: This applies to
				damage dealt by both your Wizard spells and your Wizard class features,
				which notably includes Withering Strike. Necrotic damage spells aren’t
				the Wizard’s best direct damage options, but this is extremely useful
				for your created/summoned undead.

: Animate Dead prepared for
		free, and you can treat it as one level higher if you want to. This lets you
		animate more skeletons/zombies and it lets you reassert control over more
		creatures, which stretches your spell slots a bit further. Unfortunately, it
		doesn’t benefit Create Undead, so you get more efficiency from skeletons and
		zombies than you do from cooler undead like ghouls and mummies.

The sub-features profice significant buffs to your undead. This is what
			delivers on the fantasy of commanding an army of the dead. Additional hp
			and damage mean that low-CR undead like basic skeletons are still useful
			as you gain levels.

However, none of this improves attack bonus. While Summon Undead and
			Battle Familiar will be amazing, the permanent undead that you create with
			Animate Dead and Create Undead have attack bonuses of at most +5. As enemy
			AC scales, your permanent undead will rarely be able to hit with their
			attacks.

: This adds quite a
				bit of durability to your created/summoned undead. Animate Dead and
				Create Undead give you low-CR undead that will otherwise feel very frail
				when facing your higher-CR enemies. Adding some extra hp will let them
				survive a little bit longer.

This appears to stack with Familiar Friend. If you summon an undead
					familiar, you can add a ton of additional hit points so that your
					familiar stays decently durable even as enemy damage output scales. If
					you have a +4 Intelligence modifier Familiar Friend, and a skeleton
					familiar, they wold have 35 hit points at level 6. That’s probably
					close to what you have as a Wizard.

: A decent boost to
				your undead minions’ damage output, provided that they can hit with
				their attacks. If you cast Battle Familiar on your Undead Familiar and
				also cast Summon Undead, you can apply this damage bonus several times
				in a round on creatures that already do decent damage.

: Very cool, but the
		timing is a pain. This only works when you

Bloodied, which
		means that you need to take damage while above half hp, then fall below half
		hp as a result. If you’re lucky, you could use this to heal above Bloodied,
		then use it again later since there’s no limited number of uses.

Picking an undead to consume could be difficult here. Your
			permanently-created undead cost money to create, and even Find Familiar
			has an expensive gp cost. Creatures summoned with Summon Undead don’t cost
			gold, but you probably want them fighting more than you want a few hit
			points. If you happen to have Danse Macabre running, those
			skeletons/zombies are an easy choice, but that’s such a limited and
			situatonal spell that you’ll rarely have it running. Pick whichever of
			your undead you think is most expendable or most likely to die soon
			anyway.

: Remember that you need to be holding your
		spellbook for these features to apply.

: Even more durability
				for your undead minions! Since this is a Bonus Action, you could wait to
				use it until you’re in combat or until you’ve cast Summon Undead, but
				the most reliable use is likely to crowd all of your undead minions into
				the AOE immediately after a long rest and use it then so that your whole
				army goes into the day protected.

: This lets you
				turn your undead into explosions when they die. The damage you’ll deal
				with permanently-created undead will be pitiful since they have so few
				hit dice (skeletons and zombies have just 1), but the effect prevents
				creatures from taking Reactions, which will be more impactful against
				many creatures. Unfortunately, the area of effect doesn’t exclude
				allies, so your exploding undead might become a danger to your other
				undead.

If you were deperate, you could lean into this. Have a bunch of
					skeletons and zombies crowd in around an enemy, then let them all
					destroy each other with a cascade of explosions (or drop a Fireball on
					them), each triggering their own explosion. With a 10-foot emanation,
					you can fill 24 spaces around a medium creature, turning 24 creatures
					into 24d6 damage of damage. If you have your undead intentionally fall
					prone, you can fit an unlimited number of creatures into a single
					space (yes, that’s how that works, we did a whole podcast episode
					about it).

You could, in theory, use every spell slot of level 3 and above for
					Animate Dead, create an army of skeletons, have them all pile into a
					single square next to an enemy, then drop enough damage into the
					square to kill them all and detonate them. It would be incredibly
					expensive, but sometimes you need to handle an absurd threat that
					demands an equally absurd solution. Tiamat has 615 hp, so 352
					skeletons could kill her even if she passed every save for half
					damage.

You can also use this on an enemy undead, but it’s much more costly,
					much less reliable, and you’re much less likely to have an opportunity
					to do so at a time when doing so would actually do something useful.
					If you’re going to do it at all, save it for major undead enemies with
					other nearby enemies and try to avoid bombing your own party if at all
					possible.

content.text:
The Transmuter Wizard focuses primarily on their Transmuter’s Stone, a tool
	which provide some passive buffs to whoever holds it, but they also get some
	powerful enhancement to non-offensive Transmutation spells and a unique and
	powerful way to cast Polymorph.

items.text:
: Proficiency in
		Constitution saves is huge, plus you get a second benefit of your choice.
		It’s probably best for you to hold onto the stone yourself just for the save
		proficiency, but you might share it with an ally if they’re likely to
		benefit from the damage resistance.

: Great, but you can cast
				Darkvision. It has an 8-hour duration and doesn’t require Concentration.
				Goggles of Night are an Uncommon magic item, and most playable species
				have Darkvision.

: The equivalent of
				Longstrider. Speed is nice, but it’s not nearly as impactful as the
				other options. Also, you can cast Longstrider.

: Damage resistances are
				always great, and the spells which provide them require Concentration.
				Magic items which provide damage resistances are typically Rare or
				better. If you don’t know what to pick, choose Poison, Fire, or
				Cold.

: Free spells in your
		spellbook. Always nice, but not massively impactful.

: The closest we’ll get
		to Polymorph until we’re level 9, but Alter Self is a situational answer to
		a handful of specific challenges. It is not a go-to buff, and you have
		absolutely no reason to concentrate on it in combat.

: A bit of extra
				speed when you’re swimming. Sure, why not.

: Better than
				Disguise Self, but Advantage on Charisma (Deception) won’t help much
				when you have 8 Charisma and aren’t proficient.

: Unless you
				multiclassed into Monk, you have no business using this. The problem
				with Natural Weapos isn’t the damage dice, it’s that you have d6 hit
				points and no armor. You have absolutely no reason to be fighting in
				melee.

: This affects a
		huge number of spells. Not all Transmutation spells benefit from being
		upcast, but many will add additional targets (Longstrider) or improve their
		effect (Magic Weapon).

: Strength saves are
				rare, and Advantage on a save is only useful if you have a decent chance
				to pass it. Wizards nearly always dump Strength, so that’s not you, but
				may you want to share your stone.

: An easy way to detect
				hidden and invisible enemies. If your party likes to use things like
				magical darkness or fog, you can use this to fight effectively even
				though you can’t see your targets. Many spells explicitly require you to
				see your tagets, of course, but this will at least let you aime
				Fireball.

: Polymorph prepared for free, a
		free casting once per day, and you can cast an upgraded version of Polymorph
		once per day which lets you retain your mental stats, proficiecies, class
		features, and feats, and you can cast many Transmuitation spells while
		polymorphed. Unfortunately, you can’t recharge this in any way, but
		sometimes turning into a 3 Intelligence Tyranosaurus isn’t the right answer
		and you instead need to turn into a 20 Intelligence Tyranosaurus which can
		cast Disintegrate. Just remember that you still need to concentrate to
		maintain Polymorph.

: “Similar size
				and mass and of equal or lesser value” is a pretty strict limitation. No
				lead into gold here. But you could turn a big pile of material into a
				tool or a weapon, which might occasionally be useful, or you could turn
				a door into splinters, which is a fun way to bypass a lock.
				Unfortunately, it appears that the target object needs to be a discrete
				object, not a chunk of a bigger object like a brick in a wall. If that
				were an option, you could use this to deconstruct buildings. None of
				that is likely to be worth a level 7+ spell slot, unfortunately.

: A big hit of healing, plus
				you remove a bunch of conditions which typically require Restoration.
				Heal might provide better hp restoration for the same spell slot, but
				Wizards typically can’t cast Heal.

This is notably the first thing in the 2024 DnD 5.5 rules which
					allows you to cure a Magical Affliction.

: Only situationally
				useful since you’re probably not raising the dead daily. But not needing
				to pay for the expensive material component is certainly nice.

There’s some ambiguity in the text of the rules here. Master
					Transmuter allows you to spend your Transmuter’s Stone to use these
					effects, and Restore Life specifically uses the stone in place of the
					normal material component. Master Transmuter states that the stone
					turns to dust after it’s used this way, but Raise Dead would consume
					the stone like it does with the normal diamond dust. I think the
					intent is that you can use Restore Life, but the stone is still gone
					even if you spend a level 7+ spell slot.

: You’re mostly here
				for the Exhaustion removal, which is situationally useful. Appearing
				younger is great, but it doesn’t fix things like your sore joints or let
				you outlive normal life expectancy. But, hey, at least your subjects
				will die looking youthful.

sections.heading: Legacy Wizard Subclasses: DnD 5e Subclasses in the DnD 5.5 Rules

content.text:
Not all of the subclasses have been updated to the DnD 5.5 rules. The
	assessments below reflect the existing versions of the subclasses when used
	with the DnD 5.5 versions of the base class.

When adapting legacy Wizard subclasses, subclass features granted at levels 2
	are moved to level 3.

Chronal Shift and Convergent Future feel very similar in function to the
	School of Divination’s Portent feature, and if you want that feature but don’t
	share my love for divination spells, Chronurgy Magic is a great option.
The Chronurgy Magic subclass gains access to the Dunamancy spell list. See my
Dunamancy Spell List Breakdown

for
	guidance on Dunamancy spells.

items.text:
: Rerolls are always great,
		and you can use this after the target rerolls. The target can be you, an
		ally, or an enemy, so you can use this to divert critical hits, to offer
		another attempt on failed saves, or if you’re not worried about your own
		safety you could use this to let allies reroll missed attacks. Generally you
		should save this to be used defensively. Rerolling one ally’s missed attack
		will rarely save a life, but rerolling saves will save lives constantly.

: A sizable bonus to
		Initiative. Going first is incredibly useful for spellcasters who can place
		area control effects to shape the rest of the fight.

: Taking a creature out
		of a fight for a turn is great, but Constitution saves tend to be high, and
		the effect only lasts until the end of your next turn so you’re giving up
		your Action on your turn to

deny the target their own
		turn. It’s a fine trade if your party outnumbers your enemies, but if you’re
		outnumbered you should be fireballing things rather than trading turns with
		a single enemy.

: I see four ways to use
		this:

You can have an ally cast a spell which typically affects the caster so
				that you can share powerful effects like Shadow Blade.

You can have an ally cast a concentration spell and hold the
				concentration for you. This is especially useful for familiars who can
				cast the spell then run and hide without cutting into your party’s
				effectiveness significantly.

If you’re especially cheeky and have access to the Ravnica
					backgrounds, being Orzhov and handing Spirit Guardians to your fighter
					is pretty fun.

You can use it to let another creature cast a spell for you so that you
				can get an extra spell off in a hurry. A familiar is a fantastic choice
				in this case. They’re prohibited from making attacks, but nothing stops
				them from casting Fireball.

Cast a spell with a long casting time, then freeze it upon completion.
				Carry the bead around for a bit, then activate it to deliver the
				spell.

Give every member of the party their own Familiar. Give your Familiar a
				Familiar. Give that Familiar a Familiar.

: Rerolls are great, but
		they’re still a roll. Take the risk out of it and just decide that a roll
		succeeds or fails. The cost is high, however, and it gets worse the more
		times you use this in a day. Few creatures can give you levels of
		exhaustion, so it’s usually not a problem, but the one time you encounter an
		enemy which inflicts Exhaustion you’re in serious trouble if you’ve used
		this at all that day. Also avoid things like starving, sleep deprivation,
		and forced marches. Dying at level 14 because you’re tired is hardly the way
		you want to go out.

content.text:
Graviturgy is a really cool concept, but the abilities are simply too
	situational and difficult to use to make it effective. The only reliably
	useful ability is Event Horizon, which you get once per day starting at level
	14, and even then it’s incredibly dangerous to use because you need to be so
	close to your enemies and because it doesn’t exclude your allies.

There are some abuse cases which can make Graviturgy Magic work well, such as
	throwing enemies into low-hanging AOE damage effects with Gravity Well, and
	cooperating with allies who like to grapple in order to capitalize on Adjust
	Density, but unless your party has abundant options to force enemies to either
	move or not move at your wthem, you may struggle to make the subclass features
	consistently impactful. The Dunamancy Spell List offers perhaps the most
	crucial options for the Graviturgy Magic Wizard, so if those spells are not
	available to you, I strongly encourage you to look elsewhere.

The Graviturgy Magic subclass gains access to the Dunamancy spell list. See
	our
Dunamancy Spell List Breakdown

for
	guidance on Dunamancy spells.

items.text:
: Situational. Your allies
		might enjoy the extra speed from time to time, and Advantage on Strength
		checks is great for allies who are grappling, but the 1-minute duration and
		Concentration requirement mean that you can usually find something better to
		do. Still, you can use it as often as you like and there’s no save, which is
		great if your allies like to Shove or Grapple.

: 5 ft. of positioning is
		occasionally very useful. Since this is forced movement, it doesn’t provoke
		Opportunity Attacks, so you can use this to cast a spell on yourself or an
		ally to move the target out of melee without provoking an opportunity
		attacks, and potentially breaking grapples. Tragically, it only applies when
		you cast the spell so you can’t repeatedly reposition targets to keep them
		inside areas of effect. This also doesn’t specify which directions you can
		move the target, so theoretically you could move targets 5 feet into the air
		to force them into conveniently-positioned effects like Wall of Fire.

: There aren’t many
		options which can force enemies to fall, so either you need to

like Reverse Gravity and Gravity Sinkhole, or your DM likes
		to put a lot of pits and cliffs on the map. Regardless, it’s at most 10d10
		damage per day (assuming you can somehow cause falling damage on 5 separate
		rounds) and you have to spend your Reaction to activate it each time,
		meaning that you don’t have your Reaction for Shield or Absorb Elements.

: A great area control
		effect hampered only by the fact that you need to be in the middle of it.
		With a radius of just 30 feet, you’re easily within reach for attacks and
		abilities with any sort of range, and since you need to Concentrate on this,
		you might lose your signature feature for the day if you take even a tiny
		amount of damage.

Fortunately, this doesn’t appear to care about cover, so you can do
			things like casting Stone Shape or Wall of Ice to erect a dome over
			yourself for cover, then lie prone inside it to impose Disadvantage on
			ranged attacks against you. If cover isn’t a option, try to keep moving
			enemies at bay by hitting them with things like Thunderclap to push them
			away or Ray of Frost to reduce their speed. Even Earth Thremor may be
			useful, as knocking targets prone forces them to spend half their speed to
			stand.

content.text:
If you want to collect every Wizard spell every published (like me), Order of
	Scribes is a great choice. They get some unique capabilities to address many
	challenges commonly faced while adventuring, but they’re not focused on any
	one small part of wizardry. Rather, Order of Scribes is a sort of generic
	Wizard subclass that emphasizes, complements, and celebrates some of the best
	things about being a Wizard (like collecting all of the spells). In many ways,
	Order of Scribes is the most wizard-y Wizard there is.

items.text:
: Copying a spells normally takes two hours
		per spell level. This reduces that time considerably. Time spent learning
		spells is typically handled “off screen”, but if you’re tracking Downtime,
		this means that you can copy 60 times as many spells in the same amount of
		time as other wizards.

The quill also allows you to vandalize stuff for free. The ink doesn’t
			magically adhere to things, but given time you could scribble over every
			book in a library, rendering them illegible until you decide to erase your
			scribbles. Tragically, the free ink doesn’t make it free to add more
			spells to your spellbook, so expect to spend the bulk of your money on
			copying new spells.

: The ability to change
		the damage type of your spells makes it much easier to use damage spells.
		Look for spells which deal damage types that are rarely resisted like Force,
		Thunder, Psychic, Necrotic, and Radiant damage. If you know enough spells
		and know your enemies’ resistances, you may go your entire career without
		dealing damage to a creature which has resistance to that damage type. But,
		again, you need to learn as many spells as possible to get the most out of
		this feature, so if your DM doesn’t give your access to more spells, you may
		struggle to make this work.

The third benefit lets you cast a Ritual more quickly once per day.
			That’s great for options like Detect Magic and if you need them in a
			hurry, but hopefully you won’t need it often.

: Similar in many ways to
		Arcane Eye, though certainly less subtle since it’s not invisible. This
		allows you to examine distant objects, peek around corners, keep watch in
		two places at once, and even explore small spaces where you can’t physically
		fit. It even has Darkvision even if you don’t, so it can mostly serve in
		place of your own eyes in dark places. Think of it like one of those
		quadcopter drones, but your controls only work out to a range of 300 feet
		and you can shoot fireballs through it.

You also gain the ability to cast spells using your spectral mind as the
			origin point. This allows you to cast spells while you’re safely behind
			cover, or to deliver short-range spells like Burning Hands or Thunderclap
			without the risk of being in near-melee range and potentially even without
			the targets being aware of your presence. However, the number of times you
			can do this per day is small, so look for other ways to solve the same
			problems if you can.

It’s not totally clear how this interacts with Emanations or other spells
			with a range of “self”. Emanations typically use the target of the spell
			as the origin point, so I think you can use the Spectral Mind as your
			origin point for spells like Sword Burst and Yondale’s Regal Presence.

: Since you can’t share
		this (the scroll is unintelligible to anyone else), this is basically just a
		free spell per day. Find your favorite level 2l spell with a decent effect
		for being upcast to level 3. You don’t need to have the spell prepared, so
		this is good for spells with long durations which you know you will cast,
		but which you won’t cast more than once.

: Advantage on Arcana
		checks is really nice, especially if you’re using the rules for identifying
		spells presented in Xanathar’s Guide to Everything and if your DM allows you
		to use skill checks to identify monsters and their weaknesses.

The second benefit of this feature allows you to entirely negate sources
			of damage. However, this comes with a steep cost and a gamble. First, it
			eats your Reaction, so consider using Shield or Absorb Elements if either
			of them will suffice. Second, it dismisses your Spectral Mind, so you’ll
			need to re-manifest it as a Bonus Action on a later turn.

Third, and most important, you temporarily lose access to some of the
			spells in your spellbook. This is honestly a pain to track, but it’s also
			easy to mitigate this cost. By learning a huge number of spells, you can
			accumulate enough spell levels worth of unused spells that you may be able
			to use this numerous times in succession. Just keep in mind that at an
			average of 10.5 spell levels, you need to spend an average of 525gp
			learning the spells to fuel a single use. That’s a pittance at this level,
			but you want to do it as many times as possible, which can become
			expensive.

Finally, if you roll the 3d6 and roll more spell levels than you can
			spend, you’re immediately reduced to 0 hit points. This can prevent you
			from immediately dying due to massive damage because the original damage
			is still prevented, but if the original damage wasn’t going to knock you
			down to 0, you’re going to feel silly for knocking yourself out because
			you don’t know enough spells.

content.text:
Despite the flavor text, War Magic is primarily defensive. Power Surge (and
	arguably Deflecting Shroud) are the only truly offensive abilities, and the
	damage provided is fairly small. War Magic has a lot of overlap with School of
	Abjuration, but where School of Abjuration focuses more on countering spells
	and defending your allies, War Magic focuses more on defending yourself and
	keeping yourself in a fight.

items.text:
: Shield provides a
		better AC bonus, but the real appeal here is the bonus to saves. +4 is
		enough to make a huge difference, and features that provide similar bonuses
		(The Paladin’s Aura of Protection, the Artificer’s Flash of Genius, etc.)
		are
available this early in your career.

However, Arcane Deflection comes with an opportunity cost beyond your
			Reaction: You can’t cast non-Cantrip spells during your next turn.
			Consider that casting leveled spells is your primary function as a Wizard,
			that’s a lot to give up. When you use Arcane Deflection, you need to be
			ready to spend your next turn using Cantrips or something. At low levels
			where your spell slots are few in number, that’s not a problem, but as you
			gain levels the opportunity cost grows considerably. You can’t even use
			items like wands to get around this because those items still cause you to
			cast a spell.

There may still be times where Absorb Elements or Shield make more sense
			so that you can cast leveled spells on your turn, and fortunately as the
			opportunity cost to use Arcane Deflection increases, the opportunity cost
			to prepare Absorb Elements and Shield is reduced as your number of
			prepared spells increases.

: Initiative bonuses are
		always great, and getting to go early means that you can quickly cast buff
		or control spells which will determine how the fight plays out.

: The damage isn’t great, and
		it will be hard to charge your power surges unless you’re facing a lot of
		enemy spellcasters. You could ask your allies to waste low-level spells
		(ideally a Cantrip with a non-instantaneous duration like Guidance or
		Shillelagh) so that you can dispel or counterspell them, but it’s probably
		not worth your spell slots do this in order to recharge your Power Surge
		pool.

: If you’re not maintaining
		Concentration on a spell, you should be casting a spell that requires
		Concentration. There are too many good Concentration spells for you to not
		have one running. The bonus to saves notably applies to your save to
		maintain Concentration, and combined with Arcane Deflection, you’re very
		effective at maintaining Concentration.

If you’re worried about the cost to constantly cast and maintain
			Concentration, look at summoning spells. They typically have a 1-hour
			duration and many are very effective without taxing your action economy,
			so it’s easy to fit them into your tactics. Another useful option is
			running Enhance Ability (Dexterity) so that when combat starts you or
			another party member (maybe several if you upcast it), have Advantage on
			the Initiative check.

: You only get to use
		Arcane Deflection if you’re hit by an attack or if you fail a saving throw,
		but Deflecting Shroud works even if Arcane Deflection doesn’t negate the
		effect which triggered it, so you’re always guaranteed the damage.

The damage from Deflecting Shroud isn’t great, but there’s no usage
			limitation beyond your Reaction, and since it hits three targets at range
			it can easily out-damage Cantrips. If you’re facing groups of weak
			enemies, they might hit you sheerly by making a large number of attacks or
			by including you in an area damage effect, and this may allow you to thin
			their numbers without spending expensive spell slots.

The damage also helps justify using Arcane Deflection at high levels by
			taking some of the sting out of giving up leveled spells for a turn. By
			this level, your pool of spell slots is enormous, so limiting yourself to
			Cantrips in many circumstances means that your turn is reduced to a tiny
			splash of damage where you could instead throw a leveled spell like
			Fireball or Chain Lightning.

If you want to trigger this easily, have an ally can make an unarmed
			strike to hit you for 1+Strength damage to set this off, allowing you to
			get a bunch of extra damage before a turn where you may have already
			planned to cast a Cantrip. If you don’t have an ally handy, keep an angry
			rat in a sack, stick your hand into the sack, and wait for the rat to bite
			you.
